what-is-git-and-github-install-and-setup: Git = a program on your computer that keeps the history of a project in a hidden `.git` folder. Works offline.
GitHub = a website that stores Git projects online: backup, sharing, teamwork, a place to show your work.
GitLab and Bitbucket do the same job as GitHub. The Git commands stay the same.
Tell Git who you are once: `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`
`--global` = use this setting for every project on this computer.
your-first-git-repository-init-add-commi: Three places: working folder, staging area, repository (history).
`git init` makes the folder a repository. `git status` shows what is going on and is always safe.
`git add` moves changes to staging. `git commit -m "message"` saves them as a snapshot.
`git log --oneline` shows the history, newest first. `git diff` shows what you changed.
`.gitignore` lists files Git should skip (`*.log`, `node_modules/`, `.env`). It only works on files not yet tracked.
Commit small and often. One commit = one change you can explain in a short sentence.
undo-mistakes-restore-amend-revert: Unsaved edit you want gone: `git restore file`. Careful, it cannot be brought back.
Fix the last commit: `git commit --amend`. Only if you have not pushed it.
Undo a shared commit safely: `git revert`. It adds a new commit that does the opposite.
Dangerous: `git reset --hard`, `git push --force`, `git clean -fd`. Know what they delete before you run them.
Lost a commit? `git reflog` is the safety net.
git-branches-and-merging: A branch is a movable label that points to a commit. Try ideas on a branch, keep `main` stable.
`git switch -c name` creates a branch and moves to it. `git switch main` goes back.
Switch to the branch that should receive the work, then `git merge other-branch`.
Fast-forward merge: `main` had not moved, so Git just moves the label. No merge commit.
`git branch -d name` deletes a merged branch. Git refuses if it is not merged.
Commit or stash your work before you switch branches.
resolve-git-merge-conflicts: A conflict = both branches changed the same lines. It is not an error. Git asks you to decide.
`git status -s` shows `UU` for the file with the conflict.
Open the file, choose the final text, and delete all three marker lines: `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`.
Never commit a file that still has markers. Search the project for `<<<<<<<`.
Lost in the middle of it? `git merge --abort` takes you back.
github-remotes-push-pull-and-clone: A remote is another copy of your repository, usually on GitHub. The default name is `origin`.
First push: `git push -u origin main`. `git remote -v` lists your remotes.
`git clone url` copies a whole repository with its history and sets `origin` for you.
`git fetch` downloads changes without touching your files. `git pull` fetches and merges.
Sign in with Git Credential Manager, a personal access token or an SSH key. Never put tokens in a project file or a chat.
Daily rhythm: pull, work, commit, push.
pull-requests-forks-and-code-review: Pull request flow: branch, commit, push, open the pull request, review, merge.
Good PR: short title, a description of what and why, small size, link the issue (`Closes #12`).
Read your own diff on the PR page before you ask anyone to review it.
Fork = your own copy of someone else's project. Contribute from a branch on your fork, then open a PR.
Keep a fork up to date from the original repository before you start new work.
A red check: read the log, fix, push again. Be patient and thank your reviewers.
good-commits-gitignore-and-keeping-secre: A good commit message says what changed and why, in a short line.
Small, focused commits make history easy to read and easy to undo.
Never commit: secrets, personal data, `node_modules/`, build folders, large binaries, `.DS_Store`.
Keep secrets in a `.env` file and list `.env` in `.gitignore`.
Committed a secret? Treat it as stolen: revoke it and create a new one first. Cleaning the history comes second.
A README is the front door of the project. Add a licence if others may reuse it.
stash-tags-and-exploring-history: `git stash` puts unfinished work aside. `git stash pop` brings it back. `git stash drop` deletes it.
A tag names an important moment, such as a release.
`git log --oneline --graph --all` shows branches. `git log -5` shows the last five commits.
`git show HEAD` shows the latest commit. `git diff main feature` compares two branches.
`git blame file` shows who changed each line and when. Use it to find the commit that explains a line.
`git cherry-pick` takes one commit. Use `rebase` with care, never on shared history.
git-and-github-for-your-job-search-and-c: Profile: professional username and photo, a one-line bio, links to LinkedIn or your resume.
A repository named exactly like your username shows its README on your profile.
Pin your best projects. A README needs: a one-line description, screenshot, features, tech, install steps that work, what you learned.
Never publish secrets, personal data or an employer's confidential code.
Use the GitHub no-reply email if you do not want your real email in commits.
Be honest: show what you really built, and say what you learned or what is next.
